::: {.cite-bar .domain-foreign-policy}
[In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Pub. L. 75-583]{.cite} [52 Stat. 631]{.cite} [22 U.S.C. 611-621]{.cite}
:::

A disclosure law. People who act in the United States on behalf of foreign governments, parties, or other foreign principals in political or public relations work must register with the Justice Department and report their activities and payments.

## Key provisions

- Registration and periodic disclosure by agents of foreign principals.
- Labeling of informational materials distributed for a foreign principal.
- Exemptions for diplomats, commercial activity, lawyers in legal proceedings, and those registered under the Lobbying Disclosure Act for non-government foreign clients.
- Criminal penalties for willful violations.

## Why it matters

Written to expose Nazi propaganda before the Second World War and refocused on lobbying in 1966, it became prominent again after 2016. It regulates influence through transparency where the [Espionage Act](espionage-1917.qmd) regulates it through prohibition, and it bears on the same concerns as the [Smith-Mundt Act](smith-mundt-1948.qmd).

## Current status

In force. Enforcement priorities have shifted with each recent administration.
